title: Soil in pots
teaches: The perched water at the bottom of every pot, potting mixes and their ingredients, and watering and feeding plants whose roots cannot reach any other soil

blocks.text: Garden soil that drains well in a bed often stays waterlogged once it is put in a pot. In a bed, water soaking down through the topsoil is drawn on into the drier soil below it, which keeps pulling it downward. In a pot, the soil ends at the drainage holes, where it meets open air. Water can drip out of a hole only once the mix just above it is saturated, because narrow pores hold water by capillary attraction more strongly than gravity can pull it out (Lesson 2).[^perched] After every watering, then, a layer of saturated mix sits at the bottom of the pot, known as the **perched water table**.

The depth of the saturated layer depends on the size of the pores in the mix and stays the same whatever the size of the pot. Fine pores hold water higher than coarse ones, in the same way that water climbs higher up a narrow tube than a wide one. A sieved garden loam can hold water 15 cm or more above the bottom of a pot, a peat or coir potting mix about 5 cm, and a coarse mix of bark and grit only 2 or 3 cm. The same mix can therefore drown roots in a shallow pot and suit them in a tall one, because the tall pot has far more mix above its saturated layer.[^potmodel]

blocks.caption: A pot after watering and draining, shaded dark blue where the mix is saturated and paler where it holds more air
blocks.task: Find a mix and pot height that leave at least 15% of the mix full of air

blocks.text: Gardening advice has long recommended a layer of gravel or broken pots in the bottom of a container to help it drain. Water held in the fine mix will not move into the wide pores of the gravel until the mix just above it is saturated, so the perched layer forms on top of the gravel instead of on the bottom of the pot. The gravel makes the pot shallower in effect and leaves less room for air among the roots. A square of mesh or a single curved shard over each hole keeps the mix from washing out without creating a second layer.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Water drains from a pot only once the mix at the bottom is saturated, so every pot holds a perched layer of waterlogged mix after watering.
Fine mixes such as garden soil hold a deep perched layer and coarse mixes a shallow one, and the layer takes up a larger share of a shallow pot than of a tall one.
A layer of gravel in the bottom of a pot lifts the perched layer to the top of the gravel and leaves less room for air.

blocks.text: Bagged potting mixes are designed around the perched water problem. They are made mostly from light organic materials with many large pores, so that they drain quickly after watering and still hold plenty of water inside their fibres. Garden soil makes a poor base for pots, because its fine pores hold a deep perched layer, repeated watering settles it into a dense mass, and it can carry weed seeds, pests, and diseases.

blocks.title: Potting mix ingredients
points: **Peat** moss holds many times its own weight in water and is naturally very acidic, with a pH of about 3.5 to 4.5, so manufacturers add lime to raise it to about 5.5 to 6.5. Cutting peat drains bogs that took thousands of years to form and releases the carbon stored in them, so many gardeners and some governments are moving away from it.[^peat]

**Coir**, the fibre and dust from coconut husks, holds water much as peat does and starts closer to neutral. It can carry salt from the water it was processed in, so good suppliers wash it and treat it with calcium before sale.
Composted **bark** in small pieces adds large air-filled pores and resists breaking down. Fresh bark ties up nitrogen as it rots, so check that bark sold for potting has been composted.

**Perlite** is volcanic glass heated until it pops like popcorn, and it adds air while holding little water. **Vermiculite** is a mica mineral expanded by heat into spongy flakes that hold both water and nutrient ions.
Grit and coarse sand add weight that keeps tall plants from blowing over, and they open up mixes for herbs and alpine plants that need sharp drainage.
Sieved garden compost and leaf mould can make up part of a home mix, for example one part compost, one part leaf mould or coir, and one part perlite or grit by volume.

blocks.text: After a season in a pot, potting mix has given up most of its nutrients, and its fibres have broken down into finer particles that hold a deeper perched layer. You can reuse old mix for a second year by sieving out the old roots and mixing it half and half with fresh mix or garden compost, which restores both air space and nutrients. Mix from plants that died of a root disease is better spread on a bed or added to a hot heap than reused in pots.

A pot holds only a small reserve of water for the plant growing in it. A large tomato plant on a hot summer day can use one to two litres of water, which is around half of what the mix in a 10-litre pot can supply, so pots in full sun often need watering every day and sometimes twice. Check a pot by lifting it, since a dry pot weighs noticeably less than one just watered, or by pushing a finger 2 to 3 cm into the mix. Water until a little runs from the holes so that the whole depth of mix is wetted. A peat mix that has dried out completely sheds water instead of soaking it up, and the water runs straight down the gap between the mix and the wall of the pot, so stand a dried-out pot in a bucket of water for half an hour to rewet it. Watering pots evenly also prevents most blossom-end rot on tomatoes and peppers, which usually comes from an uneven water supply to the fruit (Lesson 7).

Roots in a pot cannot reach beyond the mix for more nutrients, and every watering that drains from the holes carries dissolved nitrate away with it (Lesson 7). Most bagged potting mixes contain enough fertilizer for about four to six weeks of growth. After that, feed with a liquid fertilizer every week or two through the growing season, switching to a high-potassium tomato feed once fruiting crops start to flower, or work controlled-release fertilizer granules into the top of the mix, where they release nutrients over several months.

Fertilizer salts and the minerals in hard tap water are left behind in the mix as water evaporates, and they can show as a white crust on the surface or around the rim of the pot. Once a month in the growing season, water slowly and heavily enough that a good amount drains from the bottom, which carries the surplus salts out of the mix.[^leaching] Hard tap water also contains dissolved lime that slowly raises the pH of a mix, so acid-loving plants such as blueberries and camellias grown in pots stay greener when watered with rainwater.

blocks.title: Try it in the garden
points: Soak a kitchen sponge, hold it flat over the sink until it stops dripping, then turn it up on its end. More water drips out, because the saturated layer at the bottom stays the same height while the sponge, now taller, has more of itself above that layer.
Lift each of your pots straight after watering and again when the mix feels dry 2 to 3 cm down. After a week of practice you can judge when a pot needs water from its weight alone.
Tip a plant gently out of its pot in spring. If roots circle the outside of the root ball in a thick mat, move it into a pot one size larger with fresh mix.

items.question: Why does water stop dripping from a pot while the mix at the bottom is still saturated?
options: Capillary attraction holds water in the small pores until the mix just above the holes is saturated
The drainage holes block up with roots after every watering
Water evaporates from the bottom of the pot faster than from the top
items.why: Water leaves the mix for the open air below only when the pores above the holes are full. The saturated layer that remains is the perched water table.

items.question: The same potting mix fills a 10 cm pot and a 30 cm pot. How does the perched layer differ between them?
options: It is the same depth in both, so it takes up a much larger share of the shallow pot
It is three times as deep in the tall pot
Only the shallow pot has a perched layer
items.why: The depth of the perched layer depends on the size of the pores in the mix, so it is the same in any pot. A tall pot simply has more mix above it, holding air.

items.question: Which mix holds the deepest perched layer in a pot?
options: Sieved garden soil
A peat or coir potting mix
A coarse mix of bark and grit
items.why: Garden soil has the finest pores, and fine pores hold water highest. It can hold water 15 cm or more above the bottom of a pot.

items.question: What does a 5 cm layer of gravel in the bottom of a pot do?
options: Raises the perched layer to the top of the gravel, leaving less room for air
Drains away the perched layer completely
Feeds the plant with minerals
items.why: Water stays in the fine mix until the mix just above the gravel is saturated, so the perched layer simply sits on top of the gravel. The pot behaves as if it were 5 cm shallower.

items.question: Why do bagged potting mixes contain lime when they are based on peat?
options: Peat is very acidic, at about pH 3.5 to 4.5, and the lime raises it to suit most plants
Lime holds water in the mix
Lime kills weed seeds in the peat
items.why: Most plants grow best between about pH 5.5 and 6.5 in a potting mix, far above the natural pH of peat. Lime neutralizes part of its acidity.

items.question: A tomato in a pot was planted in fresh bagged mix eight weeks ago and its lower leaves are turning pale. What is the most likely cause?
options: The fertilizer in the mix has run out, so the plant needs regular feeding
The pot is too large
The mix contains too much nitrogen
items.why: Most bagged mixes hold enough fertilizer for four to six weeks, and watering washes nitrate out through the holes. Pale lower leaves are the classic sign of nitrogen shortage.

items.question: A peat mix has dried out completely, and water now runs straight through the pot. What should you do?
options: Stand the pot in a bucket of water for half an hour
Water it lightly every hour
Add a layer of gravel to the top
items.why: Dry peat repels water, so water poured on top runs down the gap beside the wall. Soaking from below gives the fibres time to take up water again.

items.question: A white crust has formed on the surface of a pot. What is it, and what helps?
options: Salts from fertilizer and hard water, washed out by an occasional heavy watering that drains freely
A fungus that needs a fungicide
Lime that should be scraped off and replaced with more lime
items.why: Salts are left behind as water evaporates. Watering heavily enough for a good amount to drain from the holes carries the surplus out of the mix.

learned: Every pot holds a perched layer of saturated mix after watering, because water leaves the mix only once the pores just above the holes are full.
The perched layer's depth is set by the mix's pore size, so coarse mixes and tall pots leave more room for air, and gravel underneath only raises the wet layer.
Potting mixes are built from peat, coir, composted bark, perlite, vermiculite, and grit to drain fast and still hold water, while garden soil packs down and stays wet.
Plants in pots need frequent, thorough watering, regular feeding after the first four to six weeks, and an occasional heavy watering to wash out built-up salts.

perched.title: The perched water table
perched.text: Water in a pore is pulled toward the walls by capillary attraction, which acts like a suction that is strongest in the narrowest pores. Water rises about 3 cm up a tube 1 mm wide and about 30 cm up a tube a tenth as wide. At the bottom of a pot, water can only leave the mix as drops into open air, and a drop forms only where the water is under no suction at all, which happens only where the mix is saturated. The saturated layer extends upward until the suction is strong enough to pull air into the mix's largest pores, so its height is set by the size of those pores.

potmodel.title: Modelling a drained pot
potmodel.text: The figure gives each mix a pore space, a saturated layer height, and a curve for how quickly the mix holds less water above that layer, using the shape described by Brooks and Corey in 1964 for drying soils. The values are typical of a sieved garden loam, a peat or coir mix, and a bark and grit mix. Real mixes vary with their particle sizes and with how firmly they are packed, so a particular bag may hold its perched layer a centimetre or two higher or lower.

peat.title: Peat bogs and carbon
peat.text: Peat forms in waterlogged bogs, where dead mosses and sedges rot so slowly that they pile up at around a millimetre a year. Peatlands cover only about 3 percent of the world's land, yet they store more carbon than all of the world's forests combined. Draining a bog to harvest peat lets air into the peat, so microbes start to break it down and release its carbon as carbon dioxide. Several countries, including the United Kingdom, have set out plans to phase peat out of mixes sold to home gardeners, and many manufacturers now sell peat-free mixes based on coir, bark, and wood fibre.

leaching.title: The leaching fraction
leaching.text: Commercial growers describe how much of their irrigation water drains out of each pot as the **leaching fraction**. A leaching fraction of about 10 to 20 percent, meaning that a tenth to a fifth of the water applied runs out of the bottom, is usually enough to keep salts from building up in the mix. Watering slowly, in two or three passes a few minutes apart, washes salts out more evenly than a single fast soaking, which tends to run down the sides of the pot.
